title: Final Report Index
text: Relational databases rely on well-defined structures to reduce repetition, ensure consistency, and support efficient data usage. In practice, however, data analysts work with data sets that are messy, with unclear keys. While there are existing R packages, such as testdat, that offer tools for data quality, support for functions that directly assess normal forms or assist in finding keys is limited. Our project addresses that gap by creating an R package that provides intuitive functionality for determining keys and evaluating normal forms. Our package, called NormForm, introduces a set of tools to help R users identify potential keys, test whether selected attributes are valid keys, and determine whether or not a data set satisfies the first and second normal form requirements. Collectively, these functions support more efficient data organization and improve the reliability of analyses, along with providing a structured approach to preparing data sets for relational analysis. The NormForm bridges the gap between theoretical principles and practical application, making relational database concepts more accessible to all users.

title: Final Report Index
Final Report Index
text:
Process
To develop this package, we followed a process that moved from conceptual design to functional implementation. We began by identifying the specific gaps in existing R tools related to database normalization and key identification. Once those were clarified and we established what features we wanted to provide, we drafted outlines for each function, including expected inputs, outputs, and logical steps required for functionality. A major part of this process involved translating relational database concepts, such as candidate keys, first normal form, and second normal form, into computational procedures. Plain-English logic was written before any code was written, ensuring that our implementation aligned with theoretical definitions and avoided unnecessary complexity. Testing with the chosen data sets allowed us to verify correctness and refine the functions. Throughout this process, each function was developed independently, but was designed to work together. An example of this can be seen in using is_key() inside find_keys() and using both the normal form checks. Practical considerations such as missing data and data types were also evaluated. These considerations helped guide the development of optional arguments and error messages that clarify to the user why a function fails when expected conditions are not met. Future improvements were noted for the package. These included additional customization options, more extensive testing, and more structural alignment with tidyverse.

title: Final Report Index
text:
Conclusion
While focusing on creating a package to help users evaluate normal forms and identify keys within relational data sets, the package was developed. Implementing functions that check key validity, search for minimal keys, and assess first and second normal form conditions helped us produce a set of tools that make database concepts easier to apply in everyday data analysis.
While the package currently serves as a functional foundation, there is room for future development. Adding more customization, improving accuracy through additional testing, and expanding capabilities to higher normal forms would enhance the usefulness. Together, these developments demonstrate that the package not only achieves the initial goals of evaluating normal form but also provides a robust foundation for future enhancements. This package shows that normalization concepts can be made more accessible, reproducible, and useful for real data workflows.

title: Homework 1: Reproducibility
text:
Note: This assignment is available through classmoji and must be worked on and submitted on github.


An example in reproducibility


This repository contains the Nebraskan subset from the 2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS). The BRFSS is run annually by the Center for Disease control and prevention (CDC).
You can load the data with
brfss <- readRDS("brfssNE2023.rds")
The dataset contains 12886 observations on 350 variables.
The codebook for the full data is available from https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/annual_2023.html. A copy of the site is included in the repo in the file USCODE23_LLCP_021924.HTML.
Variables names starting with X_ in the R data are listed in the codebook without the starting X, i.e. the variable X_AGEG5YR can be found as _AGEG5YR in the codebook.


Todo

Clone this repository to your local machine and open RStudio using the file reproducibility-brfss.Rproj.
Create a quarto document index.qmd. This is the file in which you should include all of your work.
Use the brfss data described above to find an age distribution of all Nebraskans who participated in the BRFSS survey. Use the variable X_AGEG5YR and show the distribution in a barchart and a table. Make sure to address in a paragraph how you deal with non responses.

Is the age of Nebraskans distributed significantly different from the nationally reported age distribution? (You could run a Chi-square test of homogeneity using chisq.test) Make sure to interpret the results.
Re-do the analysis in questions 2 and 3 by considering the survey weights X_LLCPWT. Again, interpret the results. How do you explain the differences?



Submission

Make sure that your file index.qmd contains all the details needed for me to re-run your analysis.
Ensure that the file renders without an error.

Add your file index.qmd to the repository, commit and push.

Gross on repeat
10 week sensory experiment, 12 individuals assessed taste of french fries on several scales (how potato-y, buttery, grassy, rancid, paint-y do they taste?), fried in one of 3 different oils, replicated twice.

title: Stat 471 - Analysis of Messy Data
text:
Fall 2026
TR 12:30 - 1:45 pm, Canvas
Office Hours: by appointment
Instructor: Heike Hofmann, hhofmann4 at unl dot edu



Course description

Analysis of complex, real-world data sets. Analysis techniques will vary depending on interest and availability of data sets.

Not all data lives in nice, clean spreadsheets, not all data fits in a computer’s main memory. As statisticians we cannot always rely on other people and sciences to get the data into formats that we can deal with: we will discuss aspects of statistical computing as they are relevant for data analysis. Elements of literate programming help us with making our workflow transparent and analyses reproducible. We will discuss communication of results in form of web sites and interactive web applications.


Learn how to …

compute with data to check the quality,
impute missing values, wrangle data formats, and join data sources.
write efficient and reproducible code so others are able to replicate the analysis.
pull data together to solve a contemporary problem.
use LLM bots to assess their helpfulness in different situations
publish reports on the web



More Info …
The course organization on GitHub: https://github.com/stat471-at-UNL/stat471-at-UNL.github.io
Repo that creates this website: https://github.com/stat471-at-UNL/materials
